description:
Anthony Jenkinson's map of Russia, Muscovy and Tartary, first printed in London in 1562 and engraved for Abraham Ortelius's Theatrum orbis terrarum (Antwerp, 1570). Jenkinson travelled for the Muscovy Company to Moscow, down the Volga and across the Caspian to Bukhara (1558–1559). The map shows Ivan IV enthroned, and notes on the peoples he met or heard of: the golden idol Zlata Baba, sun-worshippers, a horde turned to stone, the Kirghiz who hang their dead in trees, Samarkand and the tomb of Tamerlane, and the road to Cathay.
An AI model, Claude Opus 5.5, read the map from the David Rumsey Map Collection copy without any reference text: 63 texts, notes and names, which can be read in the panel and the tour, and 205 place names, shown under “Towns, rivers and lakes” in the filter.
Turn the sheet over for Ortelius's description of Russia, read by the same model from the Biblioteca Nacional de España copy of the 1595 Latin edition (p. 104); it is the 1570 text with two later additions to the reading list.

label.en: The Kirghiz: their rite and burial in trees

text.original:
Kirgessi gens cateruatim degit, id est in hordis. habetq;
ritum huiuſmodi. cum rẽ diuinam ipſorũ ſacerdos peragit,

text.expanded: Kirgessi gens cateruatim degit, id est in hordis. habetque ritum huiusmodi. cum rem diuinam ipsorum sacerdos peragit, sanguinem, lac, & fimum iumentorum accipit, ac terrae miscet, inque vas quoddam infundit, eóque arborem scandit, atque concione habita, in populum spargit, atque haec aspersio pro Deo habetur & colitur. Cum quis diem inter illos obit, loco sepulturae arboribus suspendunt.
text.translation: The Kirgessi people live in troops, that is, in hordes, and have a rite of this kind. When their priest performs the divine service, he takes blood, milk and the dung of beasts of burden, and mixes them with earth, and pours it into a certain vessel, and with it climbs a tree, and having made an address, sprinkles it over the people; and this sprinkling is held and worshipped as God. When anyone among them dies, instead of burial they hang him in trees.
text.commentary:
The model's confidence in this reading: high.
Its note: Seven lines without a frame, under the picture of kneeling worshippers and of bodies hung in trees (r2c5/r3c5). 'est': round s, t with a very tall looped swash. 'eóq;': an acute accent is engraved over the o. 'cõcio': stroke over o (= concione). 'rẽ', 'ipſorũ', 'fimũ', 'ſuſpendũt': nasal strokes. The stop after 'hordis' is a raised point, and 'habetq;' is not capitalised.

label.en: p. 104: What the map shows; Herberstein

text.original:
HÆC Tabula non continet totam Ruſſiam, nam deeſt Polonia
& Lithuania, quæ ſub Ruſſiæ nomine etiam cõprehenduntur:
ſed vniuerſum imperium Moſcouiæ Ducis, quod mari Glacia-
li à Septemtrione terminatur, ab Oriente Tartaros, à Meridie
Turcos & Polonos, ab Occidente verò Liuones & Sueciæ re-
gem, vicinos habet, exhibet: cuius omnes regiones ſigillatim
deſcribit Sigiſmundus Baro ab Herberſtain: ad quem harum rerum ſtudioſos
lectores relegamus. De incolarum religione, ritu, viuendiq́ue more, hæc pauca
libenter ex eodem excerpſimus.
text.expanded: HÆC Tabula non continet totam Russiam, nam deest Polonia & Lithuania, quæ sub Russiæ nomine etiam comprehenduntur: sed vniuersum imperium Moscouiæ Ducis, quod mari Glaciali à Septemtrione terminatur, ab Oriente Tartaros, à Meridie Turcos & Polonos, ab Occidente verò Liuones & Sueciæ regem, vicinos habet, exhibet: cuius omnes regiones sigillatim describit Sigismundus Baro ab Herberstain: ad quem harum rerum studiosos lectores relegamus. De incolarum religione, ritu, viuendique more, hæc pauca libenter ex eodem excerpsimus.
text.translation: This map does not contain the whole of Russia, for Polonia [Poland] and Lithuania, which are also comprised under the name of Russia, are missing; but it shows the entire empire of the Duke of Moscouia [Muscovy], which is bounded on the north by the Frozen Sea, and has as neighbours on the east the Tartars, on the south the Turks and the Poles, and on the west the Liuones [Livonians] and the king of Sweden. All its regions are described one by one by Sigismundus, Baron of Herberstain [Sigismund von Herberstein], to whom we refer readers interested in these matters. Concerning the religion, rite and way of life of the inhabitants, we have gladly excerpted these few points from the same author.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

label.en: p. 104: Religion: priests, images, baptism, confession

text.original:
In religione ferè Græcorum ritum ſequuntur.
Eorum Sacerdotes vxores ducunt. Imagines in templis colunt. Infantes cùm
baptizantur, ter in aquam toti immergũtur; aqua verò baptiſmatis ſingulis in-
fantibus conſecratur. Confeſſionem quamuis ex cõſtitutione habent, vulgus
tamẽ eam Principum opus eſſe, & ad nobiles pertinere exiſtimat. Finita con-
feſſione, pœnitentiaq́. iuxta delicti qualitatem iniuncta, ſigno crucis frontẽ pe-
ctuſq́. ſignant, magnoq́. gemitu clamant, Ieſu Chriſte fili Dei, miſerere noſtri.
Hæc eſt cõmunis illorum oratio. Dominicam enim orationẽ perpauci ſciunt.
text.expanded: In religione ferè Græcorum ritum sequuntur. Eorum Sacerdotes vxores ducunt. Imagines in templis colunt. Infantes cùm baptizantur, ter in aquam toti immerguntur; aqua verò baptismatis singulis infantibus consecratur. Confessionem quamuis ex constitutione habent, vulgus tamen eam Principum opus esse, & ad nobiles pertinere existimat. Finita confessione, pœnitentiaque iuxta delicti qualitatem iniuncta, signo crucis frontem pectusque signant, magnoque gemitu clamant, Iesu Christe fili Dei, miserere nostri. Hæc est communis illorum oratio. Dominicam enim orationem perpauci sciunt.
text.translation: In religion they follow, for the most part, the rite of the Greeks. Their priests marry wives. They venerate images in churches. When infants are baptised, they are immersed wholly in the water three times; and the water of baptism is consecrated separately for each infant. Although they have confession by ordinance, the common people nevertheless consider it to be the business of princes and to belong to the nobles. When confession is finished and a penance has been imposed according to the nature of the offence, they sign their forehead and breast with the sign of the cross, and cry out with great groaning: Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us. This is their common prayer; for very few know the Lord's Prayer.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

label.en: p. 104: Communion, feast days, the dead, Lent

text.original:
Communicant ſub vtraq. ſpecie, miſcentes panem vino, ſeu corpus ſanguine.
Pueris ſeptem annorũ porrigunt Sacramẽtum: dicuntq́. tum hominem pecca-
re. Feſtos dies viri præſtantiores, peractis ſacris epulis, ebrietate, & veſtitu ele-
ganti venerantur; vulgus & ſerui plerumq. laborant; dicẽtes, feriari & à labore
abſtinere, dominorũ eſſe. Purgatorium non credunt: pro defunctis tamẽ ſacra
faciũt. Aqua benedicta nemo ſe aſpergit, niſi à Sacerdote adſpergatur. Ieiunãt
in Quadrageſima ſeptem perpetuas ſeptimanas.
text.expanded: Communicant sub vtraque specie, miscentes panem vino, seu corpus sanguine. Pueris septem annorum porrigunt Sacramentum: dicuntque tum hominem peccare. Festos dies viri præstantiores, peractis sacris epulis, ebrietate, & vestitu eleganti venerantur; vulgus & serui plerumque laborant; dicentes, feriari & à labore abstinere, dominorum esse. Purgatorium non credunt: pro defunctis tamen sacra faciunt. Aqua benedicta nemo se aspergit, nisi à Sacerdote adspergatur. Ieiunant in Quadragesima septem perpetuas septimanas.
text.translation: They take communion under both kinds, mixing the bread with the wine, that is, the body with the blood. They give the Sacrament to boys of seven years, and they say that a person then [begins to] sin. The more eminent men, once the sacred rites are over, celebrate feast days with banquets, drunkenness and elegant dress; the common people and the servants mostly work, saying that keeping holiday and abstaining from work is a matter for masters. They do not believe in Purgatory; yet they perform sacred rites for the dead. No one sprinkles himself with holy water unless he is sprinkled by a priest. In Lent they fast for seven continuous weeks.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

label.en: p. 104: Marriage and the condition of women

text.original:
Matrimonia cõtrahunt; Biga-
miam concedunt, ſed vix legitimũ matrimonium eſſe putant. Diuortia admit-
tunt. Adulterium non appellant, niſi quis alterius vxorẽ habuerit. Mulierum
conditio miſerrrima eſt: nullam enim honeſtam credunt, niſi domi concluſa
viuat, adeoq́ cuſtodiatur, vt nuſquã prodeat.
text.expanded: Matrimonia contrahunt; Bigamiam concedunt, sed vix legitimum matrimonium esse putant. Diuortia admittunt. Adulterium non appellant, nisi quis alterius vxorem habuerit. Mulierum conditio miserrrima est: nullam enim honestam credunt, nisi domi conclusa viuat, adeoque custodiatur, vt nusquam prodeat.
text.translation: They contract marriages; they permit bigamy, but hardly regard it as a lawful marriage. They allow divorce. They do not call it adultery unless a man has had another man's wife. The condition of women is most wretched: for they consider no woman honourable unless she lives shut up at home and is so closely guarded that she never goes out.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

text.original:
Gens aſtuta & fallax, & quæ ma-
gis ſeruitute quàm libertate gaudet. Omnes ſe Principis ſeruos fatentur. Rarò
illi eſt quies: nam aut bellum Lithuanis, aut Liuonienſibus, aut Tartaris infert:
aut ſi nullum bellum gerit, ſunt in præſidiis circa Tanaim & Occan fluuios, ad
reprimendas Tartarorum deprædationes.
text.expanded: Gens astuta & fallax, & quæ magis seruitute quàm libertate gaudet. Omnes se Principis seruos fatentur. Rarò illi est quies: nam aut bellum Lithuanis, aut Liuoniensibus, aut Tartaris infert: aut si nullum bellum gerit, sunt in præsidiis circa Tanaim & Occan fluuios, ad reprimendas Tartarorum deprædationes.
text.translation: A cunning and deceitful people, and one that delights more in servitude than in liberty. All of them profess themselves the Prince's slaves. He rarely has rest: for he makes war on the Lithuanians, or on the Livonians, or on the Tartars; or, if he is waging no war, they are in garrisons around the rivers Tanais [Don] and Occan [Oka], to repel the raids of the Tartars.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

text.original:
Tunicas oblongas, ſine plicis, mani-
cis ſtrictioribus, Hungarorum ferè more geſtant: ocreas ferè rubeas eaſq́ue bre-
uiores, vt quæ genua nòn[?] attingant, ſoleaſq́. ferreis clauiculis munitas habent.
ventrem nequaquam, ſed fœmora cingunt; atque adeò pubetenus, quo magis
promineat venter, cingulum dimittunt. Iuſtitiam ſtrenuè exercent in prædo-
nes. Furta & homicidia rarò capitali pœna puniuntur.
text.expanded: Tunicas oblongas, sine plicis, manicis strictioribus, Hungarorum ferè more gestant: ocreas ferè rubeas easque breuiores, vt quæ genua nòn[?] attingant, soleasque ferreis clauiculis munitas habent. ventrem nequaquam, sed fœmora cingunt; atque adeò pubetenus, quo magis promineat venter, cingulum dimittunt. Iustitiam strenuè exercent in prædones. Furta & homicidia rarò capitali pœna puniuntur.
text.translation: They wear long tunics without pleats, with rather tight sleeves, much in the fashion of the Hungarians; boots, mostly red, and rather short, so that they do not reach the knees, and they have soles reinforced with small iron nails. They gird not the belly but the hips; and indeed they let the belt down to the groin, so that the belly may stick out the more. They exercise justice vigorously against robbers. Thefts and homicides are rarely punished with the death penalty.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

text.original:
Monetam argenteam
habent, non rotunda, ſed oblonga & ouali quodammodo forma. Pellibus no-
bilibus ac pretioſiſſimis, quæ hinc per totam Europam exportãtur, regio abun-
dat: & vbique ferè ſiluoſa eſt.
text.expanded: Monetam argenteam habent, non rotunda, sed oblonga & ouali quodammodo forma. Pellibus nobilibus ac pretiosissimis, quæ hinc per totam Europam exportantur, regio abundat: & vbique ferè siluosa est.
text.translation: They have silver coinage, not round, but oblong and of a somewhat oval shape. The region abounds in noble and most precious furs, which are exported from here throughout the whole of Europe; and it is almost everywhere wooded.
source: Read blind by Claude Opus 5.5 on 26 Nov 2026 from the BNE copy of the 1595 Latin Theatrum, p. 104; the translation was then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's English (orteliusmaps.com, Ort 162).

text.original:
Hæc omnia ex citato Sigiſmundo. Plura de his
regionibus habes apud Mathiam à Michou, Alexandrum Gaguinum in libel-
lo de Sarmatijs, Alberti Crantzij Wandaliam, P. Iouium de legatione Moſco-
uitarum ad Clementem VII. Albertum Campenſem ad eundem, & Itinera-[?]
rium Perſicum Ambroſij Contareni. Sed videndus eſt etiam Bonfinij liber I.
& II. Decadis primæ rerum Hungaricarum; item liber primus vitæ Baſilidis,
ab Oderbornio deſcriptæ. item Saxoniæ Chronicon Dauidis Chytræi.
text.expanded: Hæc omnia ex citato Sigismundo. Plura de his regionibus habes apud Mathiam à Michou, Alexandrum Gaguinum in libello de Sarmatijs, Alberti Crantzij Wandaliam, P. Iouium de legatione Moscouitarum ad Clementem VII. Albertum Campensem ad eundem, & Itinerarium[?] Persicum Ambrosij Contareni. Sed videndus est etiam Bonfinij liber I. & II. Decadis primæ rerum Hungaricarum; item liber primus vitæ Basilidis, ab Oderbornio descriptæ. item Saxoniæ Chronicon Dauidis Chytræi.
text.translation: All this is from the Sigismundus cited above. You will find more on these regions in Mathias à Michou [Maciej of Miechów], in Alexander Gaguinus [Alessandro Guagnini] in his little book on the Sarmatias, in the Wandalia of Albertus Crantzius [Albert Krantz], in P. Iouius [Paolo Giovio] on the embassy of the Muscovites to Clement VII, in Albertus Campensis [Albert Pigghe] to the same pope, and in the Persian Itinerary of Ambrosius Contarenus [Ambrogio Contarini]. But one should also see Bonfinius [Antonio Bonfini], books I and II of the first Decade of the History of Hungary; likewise the first book of the life of Basilides, written by Oderbornius [Paul Oderborn]; likewise the Chronicle of Saxony of David Chytraeus.
text.commentary: The last two works named, Oderborn's life of Basilides [Ivan IV] and Chytraeus's Chronicle of Saxony, are not in the 1570 text: they were added in the Latin editions of 1592 and 1595 (van den Broecke, Ort 162).
